buildings.name: Amphitheatrum Flavium (Titus' inauguration)

params.entrances: 80 arches: 76 numbered public entrances and 4 axial (2 ceremonial on the minor axis, 2 for performers on the major axis)
params.arena: flat arena that could be flooded for naval displays
params.upperSeating: timber maenianum summum in ligneis, unfinished

buildings.summary: Vespasian began the amphitheatre about 70-72 on the drained site of Nero's lake, paid for with the spoils of Jerusalem; it is the largest amphitheatre ever built, an ellipse 188 x 156 m on 80 radial walls. Titus inaugurated it in 80 with 100 days of games in which 9,000 animals were killed; Dio and Suetonius mention a flooded arena for a mock sea battle. At the inauguration the uppermost tier and attic were not yet finished.

phases.t: construction begins on the site of the stagnum of the Domus Aurea
Vespasian dies with three storeys built
inaugural games of Titus, 100 days

Outer wall 48-50 m high: three arcades (Tuscan, Ionic, Corinthian half-columns) and a solid attic with Corinthian pilasters, windows and 240 corbels for the velarium masts. Version 1 shows three arcades only; the Chronographer of 354 credits Domitian with completing the building 'ad clipea'.

buildings.name: Amphitheatrum Flavium (completed by Domitian)

params.entrances: 80 arches: 76 numbered public entrances and 4 axial (2 ceremonial on the minor axis, 2 for performers on the major axis)

buildings.summary: Domitian completed the attic storey 'ad clipea' and built the hypogeum, a two-level warren of corridors, cages and some 60 lifts under a timber arena floor, ending water spectacles. Seating was strictly graded: senators on the podium, equestrians above, then citizens by class, with women and slaves at the top. A tunnel led from the imperial box to the Ludus Magnus.

phases.t: attic completed and hypogeum built (Chronographer of 354)

params.entrances: 80 arches: 76 numbered public entrances and 4 axial (2 ceremonial on the minor axis, 2 for performers on the major axis)

buildings.summary: Severus Alexander reopened the amphitheatre and the repairs to the upper storeys continued into the reign of Gordian III (coins of 238-244 show it restored). Further repairs followed lightning in 250 and in the 4th century, and the urban prefects recorded them on statue bases and seat inscriptions. Gladiatorial combat lapsed in the early 5th century; beast hunts continued.

buildings.name: Meta Sudans (Augustan)
buildings.summary: Panella's excavations found an Augustan conical fountain just SW of the Flavian one, at the point where four or five of Augustus' fourteen regions met; it was destroyed in the fire of 64. Seneca knew a 'sweating meta' near his lodgings in the 60s.
scholarship: Panella (ed.), Meta Sudans I (1996)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
buildings.note: Position a few metres SW of the Flavian fountain; size estimated.

buildings.name: Meta Sudans (Flavian)
buildings.summary: Domitian's monumental fountain at the turning point of the triumphal route between the Colosseum, the Arch of Constantine and the Velia: a brick cone about 17 m high, faced with marble and crowned by a finial, water oozing from the top into a circular basin 16 m across. The cone stood to about 9 m until Mussolini demolished it in 1936.
scholarship: Panella (ed.), Meta Sudans I (1996)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

buildings.name: Colossus of Sol (in the vestibule of the Domus Aurea)
buildings.summary: Zenodorus' bronze colossus, 106.5 (Pliny) or 120 (Suetonius) Roman feet tall, was cast for the vestibule of Nero's Golden House as the emperor in the guise of the Sun. Vespasian completed and erected it in 75 as Sol with seven-rayed crown, its face no longer Nero's.

phases.t: erected by Vespasian on the Sacra Via

scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)

Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
Albertson, 'Zenodorus's Colossus of Nero', MAAR 46 (2001)
buildings.note: Placed in the centre of the vestibule court, under the later Temple of Venus and Roma.

buildings.name: Colossus of Sol (moved by Hadrian)
buildings.summary: To clear the site for the Temple of Venus and Roma, Hadrian had the architect Decrianus move the colossus upright, using 24 elephants, to a new base beside the Colosseum, which later took its name from it.

buildings.name: Colossus as Commodus-Hercules
buildings.summary: Commodus replaced the head with his own portrait, added a club and a lion at its feet and an inscription of his titles as Hercules; after his murder the statue was restored to Sol.

buildings.summary: Restored to the Sun god after 192. The Chronographer of 354 records it garlanded each year on 6 June. Its fate is unknown; the brick-faced base stood until 1936.

buildings.name: Ludus Magnus (Domitianic)

params.capacity: about 3,000 spectators in the practice arena

buildings.summary: The largest of the four imperial gladiatorial schools, built by Domitian east of the Colosseum and linked to its hypogeum by a tunnel. Cells for the gladiators on two or three storeys ringed a courtyard with an elliptical practice arena (62 x 45 m) with small stands; fountains stood in the corners.
scholarship: Colini and Cozza, Ludus Magnus (1962)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

buildings.name: Ludus Magnus (Trajanic rebuilding)
buildings.summary: Rebuilt under Trajan at a higher level, in the form now visible. Disused once gladiatorial games stopped in the early 5th century.
scholarship: Colini and Cozza, Ludus Magnus (1962)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
buildings.note: Location from Pleiades (bbox of the excavated northern half). Long axis assumed parallel to the Via Labicana (rot 100, along the major axis). Overall size after Colini and Cozza.

buildings.summary: The school for the venatores and bestiarii who fought animals in the morning shows (hence 'matutinus'), listed in Regio II. Its site, SE of the Colosseum below the Caelian, is not excavated.

Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)

buildings.name: Moneta (warehouse-mint under San Clemente)
buildings.summary: A large Flavian building of tufa blocks with small rooms around a court lies under the nave of San Clemente; Coarelli and others identify it with the Moneta, the imperial mint, which the Regionary Catalogues list in Regio III. It became the substructure of the 4th-century church.
scholarship: Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
buildings.note: Identification as the mint is debated. The church of San Clemente belongs to district D.

buildings.name: House and Mithraeum under San Clemente

params.mithraeum: vaulted triclinium-shrine inserted on the ground floor in the late 2nd or early 3rd century

buildings.summary: An insula or house of the late 1st century across a narrow alley from the Moneta, whose ground floor received a mithraeum about 200; the cult room with its benches and tauroctony altar survives under the apse of San Clemente.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
buildings.note: Ends when the first church was built over both buildings (c. 390).

buildings.name: Domus Transitoria (Palatine-Esquiline galleries)
buildings.summary: Before the fire Nero linked the Palatine to the imperial Horti Maecenatis on the Esquiline with a 'house of passage'. Its Palatine parts (the nymphaeum under the Domus Flavia) survive; the connecting galleries across the valley are known only from Suetonius and Tacitus. It burned in July 64.
scholarship: Ball, The Domus Aurea and the Roman Architectural Revolution (2003)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
buildings.note: Line entirely conjectural, from the NE corner of the Palatine across the valley and up the Oppius to the gardens.

buildings.name: Domus Aurea (Esquiline wing on the Oppius)

params.ceilings: painted and gilded vaults (Fabullus); stucco and glass mosaic

buildings.summary: The surviving pavilion of Nero's Golden House, built after the fire of 64 by Severus and Celer: a single-storey range about 240 m long facing south over the lake, with a portico along its front, a peristyle court on the west, the famous domed octagonal hall with radiating rooms and an oculus at the centre, and a pentagonal court on the east. Suetonius describes ceilings of ivory panels that showered flowers and a round dining room that turned day and night. The Flavians lived in it in part; after the fire of 104 its rooms were filled with earth as foundations for the Baths of Trajan.

phases.t: begun after the fire of July 64
Nero's death; 'at last I can live like a human being' (Suetonius)
fire; buried under the Baths of Trajan

buildings.name: Stagnum Neronis (lake of the Domus Aurea)
buildings.summary: An artificial lake filled the valley between the Palatine, Velia, Oppius and Caelian, 'like a sea, surrounded by buildings like cities'. Vespasian drained it and built the Colosseum on its bed; its edge has been found under the Colosseum's foundations.
scholarship: Ball, The Domus Aurea and the Roman Architectural Revolution (2003)
Rea (ed.), Rota Colisei: la valle del Colosseo attraverso i secoli (2002)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)

buildings.name: Vestibule of the Domus Aurea (Velia)
buildings.summary: The monumental entrance court of the Golden House on the Velia, on the axis of the Sacra Via from the Forum, framed by colonnades and centred on the colossal statue of Nero. The Flavians dismantled it; Hadrian built the Temple of Venus and Roma on its platform.
scholarship: Ball, The Domus Aurea and the Roman Architectural Revolution (2003)
Rea (ed.), Rota Colisei: la valle del Colosseo attraverso i secoli (2002)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)

buildings.name: Nymphaeum of Via degli Annibaldi
buildings.summary: A brick fountain facade with niches on the slope of the Oppius above the lake, part of the landscaped terraces of the Domus Aurea.
scholarship: Ball, The Domus Aurea and the Roman Architectural Revolution (2003)
Rea (ed.), Rota Colisei: la valle del Colosseo attraverso i secoli (2002)

buildings.name: Porticoes on the N shore of the Neronian lake
buildings.summary: Colonnades and pavilions lined the lake of the Golden House, linking the vestibule on the Velia with the Esquiline wing; Suetonius' 'buildings like cities' round the stagnum. Swept away by the Flavian works.
scholarship: Ball, The Domus Aurea and the Roman Architectural Revolution (2003)
Rea (ed.), Rota Colisei: la valle del Colosseo attraverso i secoli (2002)

buildings.name: Travertine precinct of the Colosseum (with cippi)

params.cippi: travertine bollards round the outer edge, probably to anchor the velarium ropes or control crowds

buildings.summary: A travertine pavement about 17.5 m wide encircled the amphitheatre, bounded on the outside by a ring of large travertine cippi, five of which survive on the E side.
scholarship: Rea (ed.), Rota Colisei: la valle del Colosseo attraverso i secoli (2002)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)

buildings.name: Curiae Veteres (archaic-Republican)
buildings.summary: The old meeting houses of the thirty curiae, traditionally founded by Romulus at the NE corner of the Palatine; excavated by Panella's team beside the Meta Sudans, with phases from the 6th century BC.
scholarship: Panella (ed.), Meta Sudans I (1996)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)
buildings.note: At the junction of the Palatine and the Colosseum valley (boundary with district A). Plan schematic.

buildings.name: Curiae Veteres (Augustan rebuilding)
buildings.summary: Rebuilt under Augustus, as an inscription of the curiae attests, and destroyed in the fire of 64; the site was then covered by the Neronian and Flavian works of the valley.
scholarship: Panella (ed.), Meta Sudans I (1996)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)
buildings.note: At the junction of the Palatine and the Colosseum valley (boundary with district A). Plan schematic.

buildings.name: Baths of Titus (Thermae Titi)
buildings.summary: Built quickly for the inauguration of the Colosseum in 80, on part of the site of the Domus Aurea, on a raised platform reached from the valley by a wide stair. The first imperial baths on the symmetrical plan: a central axis of natatio, cross-vaulted frigidarium, tepidarium and domed caldarium, with mirrored palaestrae on either side, as drawn by Palladio. Largely destroyed; parts of the stair and substructures survive under Via Nicola Salvi.
scholarship: Nielsen, Thermae et Balnea (1990)
Yegul, Baths and Bathing in Classical Antiquity (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
buildings.note: Plan after Palladio's drawing; dimensions approximate (about 110 x 120 m). Faces SSW toward the Colosseum on the Domus Aurea grid (rot 195).

buildings.name: Baths of Titus (dry)
buildings.summary: Out of use once the aqueducts were cut in 537; the ruins were drawn by Palladio before being largely destroyed.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Nielsen, Thermae et Balnea (1990)

buildings.name: Baths of Trajan (Thermae Traiani)
buildings.summary: The first of the colossal imperial thermae, begun after the fire of 104 that gutted the Domus Aurea and dedicated by Trajan in June 109, designed (says Dio) by Apollodorus. A bath block about 212 x 150 m stood within a walled garden precinct of some 330 x 340 m, with exedrae on the sides housing libraries or lecture halls and a great curved stand on the SW. The model for the later baths of Caracalla and Diocletian; supplied by the Sette Sale cistern. Used into the 5th century.

phases.t: fire in the Domus Aurea; works begin
dedicated 22 June (Fasti Ostienses)

scholarship: Yegul, Baths and Bathing in Classical Antiquity (1992)
Nielsen, Thermae et Balnea (1990)
DeLaine, The Baths of Caracalla (JRA Suppl. 25, 1997)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)
buildings.note: Axis about 30 degrees off the Domus Aurea grid: main entrance on the NNE (rot 32), caldarium projecting SSW for the afternoon sun (Wikipedia: caldarium on the SW side). Precinct 330 x 340 m; central block placed against the NE side as in the Marble Plan fragments and Renaissance drawings. Centre between the Wikipedia and Pleiades positions.

buildings.name: Baths of Trajan (abandoned)
buildings.summary: Out of use by the Gothic siege of 537 when the aqueducts were cut. A cemetery grew in front of the NE exedra from the 5th to the 7th century; later the ruins were quarried by the monks of San Pietro in Vincoli. The Laocoon was found nearby in 1506.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)
buildings.note: Axis about 30 degrees off the Domus Aurea grid: main entrance on the NNE (rot 32), caldarium projecting SSW for the afternoon sun (Wikipedia: caldarium on the SW side). Precinct 330 x 340 m; central block placed against the NE side as in the Marble Plan fragments and Renaissance drawings. Centre between the Wikipedia and Pleiades positions.

buildings.name: Sette Sale (cistern of the Baths of Trajan)
buildings.summary: The cistern that fed the Baths of Trajan: nine parallel barrel-vaulted chambers (despite the name 'seven halls'), each about 29.5 x 5.3 m, with staggered openings to keep the water moving, holding up to 8 million litres. In the 4th century a house was built on its roof.
scholarship: Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
buildings.note: Location from Pleiades; aligned with the baths.

buildings.name: Late antique house on the Sette Sale
buildings.summary: In the 4th century a wealthy house with an apsed reception hall and mosaic floors was built on the roof of the cistern, a typical late antique reuse of a public structure on the Oppius.
scholarship: Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)

buildings.name: Claudianum terrace (platform of the Temple of Divus Claudius)

params.arcades: two storeys of rusticated travertine arcades on the W side (visible under SS. Giovanni e Paolo)

buildings.summary: A vast artificial terrace about 180 x 200 m on the NW spur of the Caelian, begun by Agrippina for the cult of her deified husband in 54. Its west retaining wall of deliberately rough-cut travertine arcades still stands under the bell tower of SS. Giovanni e Paolo. Nero turned the east side into a fountain facade for the Domus Aurea.
scholarship: Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)

buildings.note: Bounded by the Clivus Scauri (S), Via Claudia (E), Via di S. Gregorio (W) and the slope to the Colosseum (N); centre estimated from those streets. Builder field gives Claudius as the honorand; the work was Agrippina's (no person id).

buildings.name: Nymphaeum of Nero (E side of the Claudianum)

params.niches: alternating rectangular and semicircular niches with cascades

buildings.summary: Nero cut back the Claudian temple and turned the east face of its terrace into a 167 m long brick fountain wall with niches and cascades facing the Domus Aurea, fed by the Arcus Neroniani that he extended across the Caelian.

buildings.name: Temple of Divus Claudius (Agrippina's, unfinished)
buildings.summary: Agrippina began a temple to the deified Claudius after 54; Suetonius says Nero almost entirely destroyed it. Shown as an unfinished shell.

buildings.name: Temple of Divus Claudius (Vespasianic)
buildings.summary: Vespasian rebuilt the temple of Claudius in the centre of the terrace, surrounded by a garden precinct; the Marble Plan shows a hexastyle temple set among rows of trees. Martial notes that its portico spread wide shade.

buildings.note: Temple faces W toward the Palatine (rot 265), following the travertine W front of the terrace. Dimensions estimated from the Marble Plan.

buildings.name: Arch of Constantine

params.spolia: Trajanic frieze and Dacians, Hadrianic tondi, Aurelian attic panels

buildings.summary: The Senate's triple arch for Constantine's victory over Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge in 312, dedicated for his decennalia in 315 'instinctu divinitatis'. It stands on the triumphal route between the Circus Maximus and the Colosseum and reuses sculpture from monuments of Trajan, Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius beside Constantinian friezes. Some argue that its lower part reuses a Hadrianic arch.

phases.t: dedicated 25 July for the decennalia
